extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, patent examiners, judges, and IP scholars (primarily Korea-focused, with comparative references)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural criteria for evaluating inventive step (obviousness) of patent claims and related design/trademark assessment principles, summarizing KIPO, JPO, and Supreme Court jurisprudence and guidelines. Useful for examiners, litigators, and scholars applying/assessing inventive step in prosecution and litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of decision on confirmation of scope of rights (service mark)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a registered service mark holder claims confirmation of the scope of rights for a Subject Service Mark, if sameness between the Subject Service Mark specified by the applicant and the service mark implemented by the respondent is not acknowledged, then even a final decision holding that the Subject Service Mark belongs to the scope of rights of the registered mark applies only with respect to the Subject Service Mark specified by the applicant and has no effect with respect to the service marks implemented by the respondent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Therefore an application for decision on positive confirmation of scope of rights lacks benefit of confirmation and should be dismissed if sameness is not acknowledged (citing Supreme Court decisions 2002Hu2419 and 2011Hu2626).

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal test for benefit of confirmation (service mark)
rubrics_metrics.description: The benefit of a claim for decision (confirmation of scope of rights) should be judged as of the time of the decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In principle, benefit of confirmation can be acknowledged when the Subject Service Mark is implemented as of the time of decision; exceptionally, benefit may be acknowledged if the Subject Service Mark is likely to be implemented in the future (citing Supreme Court Decision 2003Hu2836).

rubrics_metrics.name: Design creativity / aesthetic value criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: A registered design that merely imitates, converts or partly transforms the shape and figure of a prior design, and which is only a commercial/functional transformation of which aesthetic value is not recognized or merely a commonplace change/composition/conversion, lacks creativity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If as a whole the Registered Design uses usual creative means or expressions common in the design field so that aesthetic value cannot be recognized, creativity is not acknowledged and the design may be invalidated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Viewer-attention / dominant characteristic comparison (designs)
rubrics_metrics.description: In comparing designs, identify the part of the Registered Design that attracts the attention of viewers (the dominant characteristic) and compare that integrated overall impression with the prior design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: if capacitor, motor plug and DC power plug allocation on the printed circuit board is what attracts attention, similarity is judged based on distribution and dominant characteristics, not isolated minor features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minor/common variations do not confer creativity (design differences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences such as commonly used color combinations, minor slants (e.g., a 45° slant), or relocating components to positions already disclosed in the industry are regarded as simple commercial/functional changes or commonplace creative means rather than evidence of creativity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such differences (e.g., color addition, slight angle change, relocation when industry shows such variants) are treated as ordinary and insufficient to distinguish for purposes of design protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessing inventive step — basic factors (Korean Supreme Court standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventive step is denied where a person of ordinary skill in the art (POSA) can easily derive the invention after studying prior art published or practiced before the application. When determining inventive step, at least evaluate: the scope and content of the Prior Art, the difference between the subject invention and the Prior Art, and the skill of the POSA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After evaluating these factors, assess whether the POSA can derive the invention despite differences; hindsight (using the specification of the claimed invention) is prohibited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim-as-a-whole analysis (no element-by-element isolation)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim has multiple elements, the technical idea of each element organically combined as a whole is the subject of inventive step analysis; elements should not be separately analyzed to determine disclosure in the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the specific solution offered for the technical problem and the specific effect provided by the combination of elements; look for suggestion/motivation in prior art to combine features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on hindsight reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Hindsight is not permitted when assessing inventive step; examiners and courts must avoid reasoning that uses knowledge of the claimed invention (from its specification) to make prior art appear to teach or suggest the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Supreme Court authorities disallowing hindsight; conclusions of obviousness must be based on prior art and common general knowledge as of filing date, not on the later-disclosed claimed solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner procedure for determining inventive step (KIPO procedural steps)
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedure: (1) Specify the invention to be examined; (2) Specify cited inventions from the POSA viewpoint assuming common technical field/problems; (3) Choose the cited invention closest to the claimed invention and compare, treating structurally combined elements as an integrated unit; (4) Determine whether the invention could have been easily made by a POSA in view of cited inventions and common general knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection of closest cited invention and integrated-unit comparison is emphasized; structural combinations must be compared as one integrated unit (without being separated).

rubrics_metrics.name: Probable cause or motivation to combine prior art (KIPO 6.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Strong grounds for determining that a POSA would have been led to the claimed invention include: suggestions in cited disclosures, close similarity of problem to be solved, close similarity of function/work/operation, and close relevance of technical fields.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If such motivations exist in prior art, they can support a finding of lack of inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere exercise of ordinary creativity (KIPO 6.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Common improvements based on general applications of known art, reasoning from known physical properties, referring to other technical fields, selecting optimal known materials, optimizing numerical ranges, replacing with equivalents, workshop modification of a design, partially removing features, and simple change of use are considered ordinary creativity and usually render claims obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When differences between claimed invention and prior art fall only under these categories, inventive step is usually denied unless other grounds exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantageous effects as supportive evidence (KIPO 6.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: If an effect derived from matters defining a claimed invention is advantageous compared with a cited invention, that advantageous effect is taken into account as affirmative support for inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner should consider whether claimed features provide comparative benefits vs prior art as part of the assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination of inventive step for combination inventions (KIPO 7)
rubrics_metrics.description: A combination invention may be evaluated by combining more than two disclosures provided a POSA could easily combine them at the time of filing. The examiner mainly considers whether cited inventions contain a motivation or hint to combine disclosures; combination may be denied if it is not reasonably makeable by a POSA considering state of the art, common general knowledge, technical problems, trends, and industry demand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No special limit on number of prior art references to be combined, but care is required: whether combination is plausible, fields are similar, and reasonable basis exists to associate references. High numbers of combined references increase risk of ex post facto reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to assess motivation/hint for combination (KIPO 7(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the motivation/hint to combine is: explicitly taught in the prior art; inherent from the technical problem to be solved; or part of common general knowledge/empirical rules of a POSA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit cross-references in prior art are treated as explicit suggestion that supports combining; otherwise must show inherent or common-knowledge basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Synergy vs juxtaposition in combination inventions (KIPO 7(5))
rubrics_metrics.description: If a combination achieves a functional interaction producing an effect different from or greater than the sum of effects of individual features (a synergistic effect), inventive step may be acknowledged; if the combination is merely a juxtaposition or aggregation of features, inventive step may be denied if individual features are obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether combined features form a technically meaningful combination rather than a simple collection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other factual factors in obviousness (KIPO 8)
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors include: (1) If a prior art document teaches not to refer to certain prior art, that prior art does not negate inventive step despite similarity. (2) Commercial success, favorable industry comments, or long pre-filing non-implementation may be secondary evidence of inventive step but are not determinative. (3) Solving long-felt need or providing unique evidence can indicate inventive step. (4) Overcoming technical prejudice is an indicator. (5) Brand-new technologies or lack of relevant prior art suggests inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objective evidence required for secondary indicia; commercial success must be tied to technical features to be relevant; these are supportive but subordinate to technical disclosure analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notes and cautions on determination (KIPO 9)
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining inventive step in light of knowledge obtained from the application/specification, examiners may be prone to prematurely conclude obviousness (warning about hindsight). Also, product inventions that explicitly have inventive step generally imply corresponding process/use inventions have inventive step; degenerate inventions do not involve inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using the application/specification content to create hindsight; consider related process/use claims appropriately; identify degenerate inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary/secondary prior art framework and stepwise JPO test
rubrics_metrics.description: The JPO requires selecting a single primary prior art (closest prior art) and then determining whether a POSA could easily arrive at the claimed invention by applying secondary prior art or common general knowledge to that primary prior art through a stepwise analysis. The combination of two or more independent pieces of prior art should not itself be treated as the primary prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If reasoning from primary+secondary is possible, the claim lacks inventive step; if not, claim involves inventive step. Examiner must assess multiple supportive/obstructive factors and not rely on a single point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors supporting non-existence of inventive step (JPO list)
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors supporting lack of inventive step include: motivation to apply secondary prior art to primary prior art (relation of technical fields, similarity of problems, similarity of operations/functions, suggestions in prior art), design variation of primary prior art, and mere aggregation of prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner should consider these multiple viewpoints together; presence of one factor alone may be insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors supporting existence of inventive step (JPO list)
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors supporting inventive step include advantageous effects and obstructive factors such as when application of secondary prior art to primary prior art would be contrary to the purpose of the primary prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: if applying secondary art defeats the primary art's purpose, that is an obstructive factor supporting inventive step.
